results.title: Can I say "play the key role in"? [closed] - English Language & Usage ...
results.content: # [Can I say "play the key role in"? [closed]](/questions/585190/can-i-say-play-the-key-role-in). If A is the main factor in successfully doing something, is it proper to use "A plays the key role in doing something" rather than "A plays a key role in doing something" (I think the latter means A is just one of important factors, instead of the most important one)? Something can play *a* key role, but it can also play *the* key role. * Smart preparation plays a key role in giving a speech. * Smart preparation plays the key role in giving a speech. answered Feb 25, 2022 at 13:42. It is better to use 'Smart preparation plays a key role in giving a speech.'. answered Feb 25, 2022 at 16:34. results.title: prepositions - play a role as vs play a role of - English Language ...
results.content: # play a role as vs play a role of. > X also plays a role ***as*** (job-function). > X also plays a role ***of*** (job-function). As you probably know, the original meaning of *role* is a part in a play, so it does mean *does the job of*. Your asking users to choose between two wrong answers if some "job-function" is to be the object of the preposition because a "role" would indicate a *job title* (e.g., bookkeeper), not "job-function" (e.g., bookkeeping). Well, ***as*** already means ***in the role of***, so it is somewhat redundant to say *play a role as*:. Your probably want to stress that this person's contribution in the company, and this would be the meaning of ***to play a part/role in something***:. > X also plays a(n) *important/significant/key* role ***as*** (job-function). results.title: "Take the role" vs. "take over the role" vs. "take on the role"
results.content: Is there a significant difference between the three expressions, or can they be used interchangeably? Also "take on the role" sounds like a viable option to me, because I'm trying more to convey the sense of him accepting a new challenge rather than simply taking possession of something that wasn't his. If it would be a newly created role, you couldn't use "over", but the other two expressions would do fine in both situations. "To take over a role" is, as you said, to take a role that was previously occupied by somebody else, which seems to be what you're looking for, as your colleague "replaced" another worker, so he "took over" that worker's role. "To take on a role" is, again as you said, to accept the role as a challenge. I'd personally recommend "take over the role". answered Mar 11, 2013 at 15:32. results.content: # Plays a role "in" or "at" doing something? I would like to say that the *driver X plays an important role **at** modifying Y*. But my supervisor corrected me to: *driver X plays an important role **in** modifying Y*. ***play a part/play a role***. Also Google Books shows that ***play a role in*** is the more common collocation. answered Feb 26, 2021 at 23:36. I see that it sounds good to say "X plays a role in Y". But somehow it sounds better to me to say "X plays a role at doing Y". As Google Books and dictionaries show “to play a role in” (+ ing form or noun) is the more commonly used construction. Play a role “at” is not grammatically wrong, it is just much less common. ## You must log in to answer this question. Find the answer to your question by asking.
